title: Solo Dev, using Claude AI to build a game on very low-power devices
author: DeanRayGames
selftext:
Hey Everybody,

I just wanted to share with you that Claude Code can help you build, even on very low powered devices.

All I have access to is a Chromebook with 4GB of ram, and an old Note 9 with 6GB of RAM. I've come up with a pretty cool workflow to work on my solo dev gaming hobby.

1. Claude Code runs in a terminal on Crostini environment. He has full access to the linux partition, and the chromebook downloads folder.
2. The Samsung Note 9 has termux installed, and runs agents that Claude on the chromebook spawns and monitors. The extra ram helps for big asks, like compiling, which often freeze the chromebook up and crash the terminal completely.
3. Despite being a 7-year old phone, or so, it's incredibly capable at running the game, compiling, capturing video for trailers, etc. I keep it plugged into the USB. Claude communicates with it via wireless ADB or SSH.
4. A watchdog script that Claude wrote helps him monitor on the agents' work every so often, and reports to me on how things are going. I can read terminal output on the phone, and I can also see when the phone is running the game for testing and captures.
5. I also subscribe to Google AI Pro, and Claude also directs Antigravity, also running in Crostini on the Chromebook. Right now we are working on translating the game into 15 different languages! Gemini is generally much better at writing prose, in my experience. The workflow right now is that for most of the languages, Claude Opus 5.5 is doing the translation work, and Gemini Neon is checking it thoroughly. After checking the full Spanish translation, Gemini found errors in about 1/18 lines of translation, amounting to many hundreds of legitimate errors. Claude reviews the feedback and makes a final judgement call on whether the translation error it spotted was legitimate.
6. I used Gemini in the web app to do a full German translation, since it has its own usage limits separate from Antigravity. Downloaded the md files, and the notes gemini sent, and fed them to Claude, who spot checked them as they came in and integrated them.
7. I have a "low memory" guard to prevent certain operations from happening until the phone has enough memory to complete them. Compiling takes a lot of free RAM. But sometimes the memory guard is too aggressive. I've had to override it manually.
8. I limit the agents running on the phone to only 2 so I don't burn through my usage too quickly. I'm on the $100/month plan so I do have to be careful. I'm easily hitting limits now with all this translation work.

If you'd like to check out my project, I'd be honored to have your opinion of it. It's in public beta right now. I need feedback! If you have tips for me on my workflow, that's appreciated too.

This post was 100% written by a human being, but this project was basically 100% done with AI, including the trailer attached to this post.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
The memory guard being too aggressive is a real thing. I hit the opposite first: my build runs a pile of checks before it packages the game, and when they all ran at once the PC killed the build twice for memory.

What fixed it for me wasn't a guard that waits for free RAM, it was tagging the steps. Anything that uses over about a gig is marked heavy, and two heavy steps never run at the same time. Everything else runs three at a time. No more manual overrides.

The other big win was skipping work instead of waiting for room to do it. Each check remembers which files it read, and if none of them changed it doesn't run again. An edit to one game mode went from 6.6 minutes to 2.9 because only 16 of 35 checks had to rerun.

Also +1 on keeping an old phone plugged in for testing. Mine stays on the cable all day. Two things I learned: close the game and turn the screen off when it's idle, and don't trust frame times while it's charging, it throttles.

replies.author: DeanRayGames
replies.body: Thank you SO much for reading my post and giving me this feedback! I shared it with claude (of course) and he has set to work and implementing exactly what you have suggested. Awesome!!!
